topStories.headline: Alice Griffith Owner Agrees to $9 Million Settlement After Years of Code Violations and Rodent Infestations
topStories.dek: Developer McCormack Baron Salazar will pay city penalties and fund mandatory repairs at the 337-unit Bayview complex in what City Attorney David Chiu called the first code-enforcement settlement in city history to direct money straight into a property.
topStories.body:
St. Louis–based developer McCormack Baron Salazar has agreed to pay $9 million to the City of San Francisco to resolve years of documented health and safety violations at Alice Griffith Apartments, a 337-unit affordable housing complex in the Bayview neighborhood. City Attorney David Chiu announced the settlement on August 26 alongside Mayor Daniel Lurie and Supervisor Shamann Walton. The deal was approved by the complex's investors on August 21 and by the city three days later; the city has since filed a stipulated injunction in San Francisco Superior Court to make the terms enforceable by a judge.

The complex opened in 2017 after a federally backed public-private redevelopment of the former Double Rock public housing site, but deteriorated rapidly after the transition to private management. Mission Local documented rat infestations, piles of debris, broken elevators, plumbing failures severe enough to send sewage backing into bathtubs, and electrical and fire-code violations affecting hundreds of low-income families. According to settlement documents, owners have resolved 31 of 41 notices of violation. The city attorney's office said McCormack Baron Salazar violated multiple city codes, state housing law, and California's unfair competition law.

Under the agreement, McCormack Baron Salazar must invest $3 million directly into pest control, security upgrades, and other property repairs over the next two years. Separately, the Mayor's Office of Housing and Community Development will contribute $2 million to improve outdoor play areas on the property. Chiu called it the first code-enforcement settlement in city history requiring a landlord not only to pay penalties but to invest additional money into the property beyond what the city had cited. The complex received $68.3 million in public loans when it was built, plus a $30.5 million federal Choice Neighborhood grant.

For many tenants, the news brought relief mixed with skepticism. Falaofuta Satele, a 30-year resident, told Mission Local she was shocked — then disappointed — noting that residents had watched repair pledges stall before, and asking why money would not flow directly to those who endured years of uninhabitable conditions. Supervisor Walton pledged his office would continue monitoring the property and tracking how improvement funds are spent.

topStories.headline: Nine New Bayview Businesses Are Opening on Third Street This Fall, Led by Bayview Oyster Bar
topStories.dek: City Storefront Opportunity Grants totaling $800,000 are fueling a wave of new openings on Bayview's main commercial corridor, including a seafood restaurant from a Bayview-born restaurateur opening this month.
topStories.body:
A wave of new restaurants and businesses is arriving on Third Street in Bayview–Hunters Point this fall, backed by Mayor Daniel Lurie's Storefront Opportunity Grant program, which has directed $800,000 to nine new businesses on the corridor — the second-largest neighborhood allocation in the program citywide after downtown. The grants, ranging from $50,000 to $100,000, cover tenant improvements, equipment, inventory, and permits.

Opening this month at 5114 Third Street is Bayview Oyster Bar, from April Spears, a Bayview native whose previous Auntie April's Chicken-N-Waffles was a neighborhood institution. Spears is combining Northern California seafood — Dungeness crab, king salmon, and oysters — with her Louisiana roots, including preparations over open flames in a New Orleans style. The space will include a raw bar, a seafood counter, roughly 25 dining seats, and eventually a backyard patio, with historic photographs of the Bayview displayed throughout.

Also slated to open on the corridor are Panamanian fusion restaurant Properly Seasoned Kitchen, Ethiopian fast-casual Moya Bayview, smoked meat specialist Phatwood Smokehouse Deli, breakfast spot Bayside Café, a café and listening lounge from Third House Coffee, and Chapter 3 — a Black-owned bookstore and wine bar from Smoke Soul Kitchen owner Vanessa Lee. Lee filed permit applications in July, telling Mission Local she was inspired by Marcus Books, the historic Black-owned bookstore that once anchored the Fillmore. She plans to open before the end of 2026.

The nine grants represent part of the city's broader investment in Third Street as a walkable commercial corridor. The grant program required applicants to already hold a signed lease and to apply within a six-week window — conditions some business owners described as challenging — but recipients say the funding has made openings possible that might otherwise have stalled for years.

topStories.headline: Crocker Amazon's $50 Million Renovation Awaits Board of Supervisors Vote as Community Opposition Continues
topStories.dek: After the Recreation and Park Commission voted in April to recommend accepting a $28 million San Francisco Giants grant for a synthetic-turf overhaul of Crocker Amazon Park, opponents have organized a public meeting at the Excelsior Library on September 26.
topStories.body:
The proposed $50 million overhaul of Crocker Amazon Park's baseball and softball complex remains before the San Francisco Board of Supervisors, which must vote to formally accept a $28 million grant from the San Francisco Giants before construction can proceed. The Recreation and Park Commission voted unanimously in April to recommend accepting the grant and to approve an accompanying public-private partnership agreement. If the Board signs off, the Giants have agreed to name the renovated complex the Willie Mays Fields of Champions, with Mays' Say Hey Foundation contributing a $5 million lead gift.

The remaining $22 million in city funds would come primarily from the 2020 Health and Recovery Bond, though the city has not yet identified the source of all of that share. Rec and Park estimates the new synthetic-turf fields — replacing natural-grass surfaces that close frequently due to poor drainage and gopher damage — could add up to 10,000 additional hours of play time each year. Design work is expected to continue through 2026, with construction tentatively starting in 2027 and completion targeted for 2028–29.

The plan has drawn sustained opposition from Keep Crocker Real, a resident coalition that objects to removing roughly 120 mature trees, installing artificial turf in a neighborhood it says already lacks natural green space, and bright nighttime lighting that would affect adjacent homes. The group is lobbying for a citywide moratorium on synthetic turf pending further health review, preparing to challenge the project's environmental impact report once it is released, and distributing information packets to all 11 members of the Board of Supervisors.

Residents who want to weigh in can attend a public community meeting organized by Keep Crocker Real on Saturday, September 26, from 2 to 4 p.m. at the Excelsior Branch Library, 4400 Mission Street. The Board of Supervisors vote has not yet been scheduled.

events.title: Visitacion Valley Night Market
events.location: Leland Avenue between Bayshore Boulevard and Peabody Street, Visitacion Valley
events.description: The second date of Visitacion Valley's inaugural monthly night market series brings free food vendors, live music, local shopping, street dancing, and community resources to Leland Avenue. Free admission; all ages welcome.

moreNews.headline: Visitacion Valley Students Get New One-Seat Muni Ride to Francisco Middle School
moreNews.body: A service change that took effect the week of August 27 gives Visitacion Valley students a direct one-seat ride to Francisco Middle School, eliminating the transfer from the 8AX Bayshore Express that riders previously had to make. The SFMTA's transit advisory dated August 27, 2026, also included schedule improvements on the 22 Owl to make it more reliable. The agency said the changes were based on rider feedback, operator input, and service data. Details are available at SFMTA.com/ServiceChanges.

restaurants.name: Old Skool Cafe
restaurants.description: A 1920s speakeasy-themed supper club run by at-risk and formerly incarcerated youth, serving global soul food and live jazz every night it's open.

restaurants.name: Gumbo Social
restaurants.description: Chef Dontaye Ball's Bayview brick-and-mortar serves acclaimed build-your-own gumbo, po'boys, and smoked meats; recently reopened after a six-week retooling.

restaurants.name: All Good Pizza
restaurants.description: A beloved outdoor pizza spot in a sun-drenched garden, serving thin-crust Neapolitan pies made with organic, locally sourced ingredients; open Tuesday–Saturday.

restaurants.name: Gratta Wines
restaurants.type: Urban winery, wine bar & Italian market
restaurants.description: San Francisco's last mainland urban winery, founded in 2006 by Barbara Gratta, offering Dry Creek Valley wines, Italian small bites, and a specialty market on Third Street.

restaurants.name: Cafe Alma
restaurants.description: A welcoming community café on Third Street in the Bayview, serving coffee, food, and hosting local events and creative workshops.

restaurants.name: Beep's Burgers
restaurants.description: An Ocean Avenue institution since 1962, serving juicy burgers, curly fries, legendary garlic fries, and milkshakes at a retro drive-in counter open daily until 2 a.m.

restaurants.name: Ocean Ale House
restaurants.description: Ingleside's social anchor at 1314 Ocean Avenue, with rotating craft beers on tap, pub food, a small live-music stage, open mic nights, and a welcoming all-ages atmosphere.

restaurants.name: Megan's Table
restaurants.description: A family-run café on Ocean Avenue serving Thai and Cambodian dishes including cha kroeung, papaya salad, pad see ew, and Tom Kha soup in a warm, plant-filled setting.

restaurants.name: Pho Golden
restaurants.description: A casual Excelsior Vietnamese restaurant well-regarded for its pho and dishes featuring grilled pork.

restaurants.name: Calabria Brothers
restaurants.description: An Excelsior Italian deli counter known for oversized, generously filled sandwiches made to order.

restaurants.name: Restaurante Familiar
restaurants.description: An Excelsior neighborhood staple serving Salvadoran and Mexican fare with praised entrees at family-friendly prices.

restaurants.name: Los Planes de Renderos
restaurants.description: A popular Excelsior Salvadoran spot focused on pupusas and traditional Central American comfort food.

restaurants.name: Don Chuy's
restaurants.description: A beloved Excelsior corner store recognized for its outstanding carnitas burrito.

restaurants.name: 7 Mile House
restaurants.description: A Visitacion Valley landmark at Bayshore Boulevard and Geneva Avenue, one of San Francisco's oldest continuously operating bars, still serving drinks on the same corner for generations.

restaurants.name: Pakwan
restaurants.description: A reliable Ocean Avenue spot for tandoori chicken, chicken achar, and hearty Pakistani and Indian dishes served in generous portions.

shops.name: SCRAP (Scroungers' Center for Reusable Art Parts)
shops.description: San Francisco's beloved 50-year-old nonprofit creative reuse depot, now in a permanent new home at 141 Industrial Street — five times the size of its former warehouse — selling donated materials at low cost to artists, teachers, and makers.

shops.name: Flora Grubb Gardens
shops.description: A beloved open-air destination garden center at 1634 Jerrold Avenue in the Bayview, widely regarded as one of the finest plant shops in the Bay Area.

shops.name: Meizzei Hardware
shops.description: A legacy hardware store on the Third Street corridor that has served the Bayview community for decades.

shops.name: Ocean Subs
shops.description: An Excelsior lunch staple praised for its Original Sub on toasted Dutch crunch, stacked with Italian meats and a tangy herb vinaigrette.

artEntertainment.name: Ruth Williams Opera House (Bayview Opera House)
artEntertainment.type: Historic performing arts and cultural center
artEntertainment.description: San Francisco's oldest extant theater and Landmark #8, the Ruth Williams Opera House is the cultural anchor of Bayview–Hunters Point, hosting concerts, theater, Stoop Sessions, community events, and youth arts programs.

artEntertainment.name: Jerry Garcia Amphitheater
artEntertainment.description: A free outdoor amphitheater named for the late Grateful Dead frontman, set within McLaren Park and hosting summer concerts and community performances.
artEntertainment.address: 100 John F. Shelley Dr, McLaren Park

artEntertainment.name: Quesada Gardens
artEntertainment.description: A vibrant community-built gathering space at Quesada Avenue and Newhall Street, transformed since 2006 with greenery, colorful murals, and tiled stairs.

gymsRecreation.name: Excelsior Yoga
gymsRecreation.description: A boutique Excelsior studio on the third floor of the US Bank Building on Mission Street, offering classical 90-minute Hatha yoga classes blended with science, pranayama, and meditation.

gymsRecreation.name: John McLaren Park
gymsRecreation.description: San Francisco's second-largest park, spanning Visitacion Valley and the Excelsior with over seven miles of trails, a swimming pool, tennis and basketball courts, a golf course, soccer fields, playgrounds, and the Jerry Garcia Amphitheater.

gymsRecreation.name: Crocker Amazon Playground
gymsRecreation.description: A large southern San Francisco park featuring a skate park, lighted soccer fields, basketball and tennis courts, children's play areas, and baseball and softball fields currently in a renovation planning process.

gymsRecreation.name: India Basin Shoreline Park
gymsRecreation.description: A newly developed waterfront park on the Bayview shore offering San Francisco Bay views, restored native habitat, and public shoreline access.
